videos.title: Why count++ lies: three steps, two threads, one lost update
Two locks taken in opposite orders: the wait-for cycle, and one global lock order that breaks it
Why the stop loop spins: the caches agree, the store buffer drains, the JIT keeps stop in a register
A volatile write and a read of the same field make a happens-before edge; a different field makes none
Seven tasks through the four rules of ThreadPoolExecutor, then an unbounded queue that makes max useless
Virtual threads mount on carriers, unmount at a blocking call, and come back on any carrier
Two consumers, one payment: notifyAll wakes both, so a woken thread must check again in a while loop
Two threads read 41, one compare-and-set wins, the other fails, reads 42 and retries
thenApply maps, thenCompose flattens a future of a future, thenCombine waits for two futures started side by side
On JDK 21 to 23 a virtual thread pinned inside synchronized blocks its carrier; with ReentrantLock it unmounts
Each worker forks onto the top of its own deque, an idle worker steals the biggest task from the bottom, and fork, compute, join keeps the halves parallel
Publishing is a write: a reader can see the reference before the constructor's field writes, unless an edge or final fields stop it
The ledger you build, sitting by sitting: locks in id order, a bounded pool, a virtual-thread front, and the earlier lesson behind each part
A thread's six states as places on a map, the call behind each move, and interrupt as a note the thread must notice and put back
Hashing stops getting faster at one thread per core, a thread that waits frees its core, and 400 requests a second for 250 ms keep 100 in flight
volatile keeps every read fresh and every write visible, yet two threads still read 41 and both write 42: the fix is one atomic step
A scope owns its subtasks like a tree: the first failure cancels the sibling, join throws at once, close waits for every branch, and a scoped value is read down the tree
After one 250 ms run, fixed rate runs the overdue tasks back to back while fixed delay shifts every later run, and a run that throws ends the schedule without a word
A latch opens for good at zero, a barrier lets a full group through and closes again, and a semaphore hands out permits anyone can give back
A bounded queue makes the fast producer wait, and one poison pill per consumer, put after the last producer, stops every writer cleanly
A monitor is a room with one key: one thread inside, the rest BLOCKED in the entry set, each unlock hands its writes to the next lock, and the owner can walk back in
get then put leaves a gap where a second thread reads the old total; merge reads, adds and writes under one bin lock, while writes to other bins run in parallel
A 200 ms request that waits 195 ms holds one platform thread the whole time, so 200 threads top out at 1,000 a second while most of them just wait

ReentrantLock is the same room with controls on the door: tryLock with a timeout and lockInterruptibly let a waiter leave, each Condition is its own waiting room, and readers share while the writer waits for an empty room
A race needs state that is shared and changing: take away either one, and there is nothing to lock
cancel(true) only raises the interrupt flag: a task blocked in sleep stops, a loop that checks the flag stops, a loop that never looks runs on, and every Future says cancelled at once
A failure skips every stage until a handler catches it, orTimeout fills the future but leaves the call running, and a handle on each call keeps one bad answer from failing allOf

Without volatile, a reader on the lock-free fast path can see the reference before the constructor's write; volatile adds the release and acquire, and a holder class lets class initialization do the locking
A virtual thread per payment is cheap but the database has 20 connections: a shared Semaphore hands out 20 permits, waiters park for the price of a heap object, and release wakes the next one

A new platform thread per tiny task costs far more than the task, a pool reuses a few workers that loop on one queue, shutdown lets the queue drain, shutdownNow hands it back and interrupts, and only awaitTermination waits
Payments outrun two threads: an unbounded queue accepts everything while time in queue climbs, a queue of four rejects at once, and four dashboard numbers plus named threads show what is happening
A thread is one walker through your code with its own stack, all threads share one heap, cores take turns or run at once, and only start() makes a new thread
A VarHandle puts the memory mode on each access: plain, opaque, release/acquire and volatile as a ladder, where a release hands everything written before it to the acquire that sees it

Two test threads that never overlap catch nothing: a start latch, more threads than cores and many rounds make them collide, a latch with a deadline replaces the sleep, and jcstress counts every outcome
A fixed pool of 10 also kept the database to 10 callers; virtual threads drop that limit and 300 requests hit 10 connections, a semaphore writes it back, and Little's law shows where requests wait
A balance sum read one locked account at a time is torn; copy every balance under every lock into an immutable snapshot and publish it with one volatile write, so readers see old or new, never a mix
